# Backup {visibility="uncounted"}

## What modelling evidence has to be {visibility="uncounted"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- **Timely.** Evidence that arrives after the decision has been taken
  is not evidence
- **Rigorous.** Explicit about methods and limitations, and as simple
  as it can be without misleading
- **Collaborative.** Several kinds of expertise have to reach the same
  model, and the people holding them are not the same people

::: {.callout-important}
Most approaches manage two of the three.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](../figures/composable-whitty.png){width="100%"
fig-alt="Whitty 2015 editorial on academic papers and health policy"}

::: {.attribution}
Whitty (2015),
[doi:10.1186/s12916-015-0544-8](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12916-015-0544-8)
:::
:::
::::

## Joint models work, and they do not transfer {visibility="uncounted"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
- England's COVID-19 models fitted cases, prevalence, severity, and bed
  occupancy together, and that evidence reached policy
- Each took expertise across several domains, and a long time
- In 2022 mpox spread through sexual contact networks. Those models
  were not adapted to it, and new single-source models were built
  instead, at speed

::: {.callout-important}
The trade-off is not between good and bad models. It is between
rigour and being able to move.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
![](../figures/composable-birrell.png){width="100%"
fig-alt="Results from the England COVID-19 joint model"}

::: {.attribution}
Birrell et al. (2025),
[doi:10.1093/jrsssa/qnaf030](https://doi.org/10.1093/jrsssa/qnaf030)
:::
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
![](../figures/composable-endo.png){width="100%"
fig-alt="Results from the 2022 mpox sexual contact network model"}

::: {.attribution}
Endo et al. (2022),
[doi:10.1126/science.add4507](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.add4507)
:::
:::

## Chaining models loses information {visibility="uncounted"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
- The ONS COVID-19 Infection Survey tested over four million swabs from
  more than 150,000 households at a cost above £500 million. Modellers
  outside saw the published prevalence, not the swabs
- Prevalence fed incidence and $R_t$, and those fed variant
  transmissibility and severity
- Uncertainty was approximated at each step and assumptions were
  inherited unchecked
- Chaining steps like these can bias the result and understate the
  uncertainty. Fitting them together instead is the fix

::: {.callout-important}
Joint fitting is the fix, and it hands you a model nobody can take
apart.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
![](../figures/composable-ons-cascade.jpg){width="94%"
fig-align="center"}

::: {.attribution}
The chain fitted as one model instead. Prevalence (A), incidence (B),
antibody prevalence (C) and $R_t$ (D) estimated together from the
survey data. Abbott and Funk (2022),
[doi:10.1101/2022.03.29.22273101](https://doi.org/10.1101/2022.03.29.22273101).
Survey figures from the paper's introduction
:::

![](../figures/composable-lison.png){width="46%"}

::: {.attribution}
The bias claim is Lison et al. (2024), nowcasting $R_t$ from line list
data.
[doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1012021](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1012021)
:::
:::
::::

## Other ways to do this {visibility="uncounted"}

- AlgebraicJulia gives formal compositional guarantees and little
  support for probabilistic models
- `JuliaBUGS.jl` and `RxInfer.jl` specify models as graphs
- `ModelingToolkit.jl` composes acausal components symbolically
- `Gen.jl` composes through nested generative functions, at a lower
  level than Turing.jl

::: {.callout-note}
Each trades some flexibility for structure.
:::

::: {.attribution}
The paper's discussion of alternative designs,
[doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17884675](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17884675)
:::

## What composable modelling would need {visibility="uncounted"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
- **Uncertainty and inference.** Propagate it properly; swap the
  inference method
- **Model structure.** Separate infection, latent, and observation
  processes; nest models inside models
- **Population heterogeneity.** Stratify any component without hand
  managing the bookkeeping
- **Accessibility and interoperability.** Components carry their
  priors, work standalone, and talk to the rest of Julia
- **Workflow.** One specification for simulation and for inference

::: {.attribution}
Table 1 of the paper sets out six themes, condensed to five bullets
here, with accessibility and interoperability merged. Each design
consideration is paired with the problem that motivates it. These came
from the authors and have had no community input.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](../figures/composable-requirements.png){width="100%"
fig-alt="Table 1 of the paper, proposed requirements with motivating
problems"}
:::
::::

## Why keep the parts small {visibility="uncounted"}

- The component structure is what makes this tractable for a language
  model to assemble. That is a reason to keep the parts small
- In multi-model work, shared parts would let you attribute a
  difference in results to an assumption rather than to an
  implementation

::: {.attribution}
Both claims are in the paper's discussion. Neither has been tested.
:::

## Reusing an AR(2) for South Korea {visibility="uncounted"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- The first replication takes the AR(2) from the worked example, a
  renewal process with a discretised serial interval, and a negative
  binomial observation model
- **A** to **C** are prior predictive checks on each part, **D**
  compares the continuous serial interval with its discretised form
- **E** and **F** recover the paper's finding. $R_t$ in South Korea
  peaked near 10 and dropped below 1 in early March 2020

::: {.attribution}
Replicating [Mishra et al. (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.16487).
Figure from the paper
:::
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](../figures/composable-mishra.png){width="88%" fig-align="center"}
:::
::::

## Swapping the infection process for an ODE {visibility="uncounted"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- The third replication drops the renewal process and uses an SIR model
  built with `ODEProcess` over the SciML solvers instead
- Everything downstream is unchanged. A Poisson observation model, and
  a second version wrapping it in `Ascertainment` driven by an AR(1)
- **C** shows both recovering $R_0 \approx 2$. **E** and **F** show the
  deterministic fit is the worse calibrated of the two

::: {.attribution}
Replicating Chatzilena et al. (2019),
[doi:10.1016/j.epidem.2019.100367][chatzilena].
Figure from the paper
:::
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](../figures/composable-sir.png){width="88%" fig-align="center"}
:::
::::
